entities.name: Vicedomino de Vicedominis
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Vicedomino de Vicedominis, an Italian cardinal-bishop from Piacenza, achieved a unique and historically significant status in September 1276 when he was elected to the papacy, only to die before his election could be formally announced or his consecration completed. As a nephew of Pope Gregory X, his ecclesiastical career was propelled by familial connections, culminating in his elevation to cardinal-bishop of Palestrina on 3 June 1273. His brief, unfulfilled pontificate occurred during a tumultuous period for the Holy See, characterized by rapid successions and the nascent implementation of new electoral procedures.

Following the deaths of Pope Innocent V and Pope Adrian V earlier in 1276, Vicedomino participated in the third papal conclave of that year, convened in Rome. On or about 5 September 1276, he was elected supreme pontiff by the College of Cardinals. However, just eight days later, on 13 September, Vicedomino de Vicedominis passed away. This premature death rendered his election void and prevented him from ever being officially recognized or consecrated as Pope, making him one of the most prominent examples of an 'un-reigning' pope-elect in history.

His passing necessitated yet another papal conclave, further contributing to the extraordinary instability of 1276, famously known as the 'Year of Four Popes' (Gregory X, Innocent V, Adrian V, and John XXI). The episode underscored the inherent fragility of papal succession during the High Middle Ages, highlighting the challenges in stabilizing the Church's leadership even after the Second Council of Lyon (1274) had established clearer rules with the constitution *Ubi periculum*. Vicedomino's 'non-papacy' indirectly reinforced the urgency for more robust and resilient electoral processes.

His case is a notable example of an elected pontiff who never reigned.
